messages.body_plain:
Hi

Reading these exchanges, I am curious as to exactly what problems these parameters can provide solutions to? Is it possible to share some code of examples where the current samplers struggle? I can't help thinking that optimal values for nadaptSN  and nadaptPN will be specific to (i) the specific problem (ii) the specific starting values, and (iii) the specific random seed. It seems hard then to have general guidelines about how to optimally set these parameters without knowing more about what issues they are trying to overcome.

Regarding nadaptSN I can think of one example where it might help, that is when starting values are very far from the target distribution (i.e. provide an extremely unlikely sample) and the direction in which the sampler climbs the likelihood mountain to arrive in the vicinity of the target submit is completely different to the direction the sampler needs to be sampling once on the summit. In this case, a sampling scheme will want to remain flexible until it is sure that it has become close to the mode and become less flexible once the covariance of the proposal starts to provide efficient sampling around the mode. The trouble is, in most real world situations the user has no idea exactly how many iterations that is going to take, and so a smarter solution is to try to detect when to start reducing the flexibility of the adaptation process. I have some Nimble code that does this if anyone is interested. I would be interested to see if there are other examples (where adjusting nadaptSN  can help) though and to test my code on them.

Regarding nadaptPN, the only instance I can imagine where this might help is where you are sure the starting values constitute a highly likely sample from the target distribution (i.e. toy problems) and there is some kind of likelihood trap (such as a degenerate solution) which you are trying to avoid the sampler's covariance adapting to - in which case modifying the model would normally be a more reasonable solution. Do you have other examples, ideally with reusable code, where nadaptPN can be useful? Again, I suspect finding optimal values in real world applications could be challenging and some sort of automation scheme might be preferable to setting fixed values in an ad hoc manner.

Best
David

Thanks everyone for the comments and input.  I agree, this is worth discussion on the possible uses of these options, and not to mention the selection of naming of the options themselves.

That said, in order to get Frédéric up and running with these ideas, I've gone ahead and implemented a variation of the standard M-H "RW" sampler, which is called "RW2", which has 3 new control options (the default value for each of these is 0).  I've also provided quick code showing how to use the RW2 sampler, below.  The new options are:

(1) niterNoUpdateTarget: Number of initial MCMC iterations during which the sampler will not update the target parameter (i.e., not sample it), nor do any adaptation.

(2) niterNoAdaptation: Number of initial MCMC iterations for which the sampler will not update the "scale" parameter, i.e. the standard deviation of the normal M-H proposal distribution.

(3) niterNoAdaptiveDecay: Number of initial MCMC iterations during which the "adaption clock" will not proceed forward, i.e., no gradual decay occurs in the magnitude of the adaptation of the "scale" parameter.

Similiar changes can readily be made to the RW_block sampler.  Questions are welcomed.

Cheers, keep in touch,

Daniel

library(nimble)

RW2 <- nimbleFunction(
    name = 'RW2',
    contains = sampler_BASE,
    setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
        ## control list extraction
        logScale      <- if(!is.null(control$log))           control$log           else FALSE
        reflective    <- if(!is.null(control$reflective))    control$reflective    else FALSE
        adaptive      <- if(!is.null(control$adaptive))      control$adaptive      else TRUE
        adaptInterval <- if(!is.null(control$adaptInterval)) control$adaptInterval else 200
        scale         <- if(!is.null(control$scale))         control$scale         else 1
        niterNoUpdateTarget  <- if(!is.null(control$niterNoUpdateTarget))  control$niterNoUpdateTarget  else 0
        niterNoAdaptation    <- if(!is.null(control$niterNoAdaptation))    control$niterNoAdaptation    else 0
        niterNoAdaptiveDecay <- if(!is.null(control$niterNoAdaptiveDecay)) control$niterNoAdaptiveDecay else 0
        ## node list generation
        targetAsScalar <- model$expandNodeNames(target, returnScalarComponents = TRUE)
        calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)
        ## numeric value generation
        scaleOriginal <- scale
        timesRan      <- 0
        timesAccepted <- 0
        timesAdapted  <- 0
        optimalAR     <- 0.44
        gamma1        <- 0
        ## checks
        if(length(targetAsScalar) > 1)   stop('cannot use RW sampler on more than one target; try RW_block sampler')
        if(model$isDiscrete(target))     stop('cannot use RW sampler on discrete-valued target; try slice sampler')
        if(logScale & reflective)        stop('cannot use reflective RW sampler on a log scale (i.e. with options log=TRUE and reflective=TRUE')
    },
    run = function() {
        timesRan <<- timesRan + 1
        if(timesRan > niterNoUpdateTarget) {
            currentValue <- model[[target]]
            propLogScale <- 0
            if(logScale) { propLogScale <- rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = scale)
                           propValue <- currentValue * exp(propLogScale)
                       } else         propValue <- rnorm(1, mean = currentValue,  sd = scale)
            if(reflective) {
                lower <- model$getBound(target, 'lower')
                upper <- model$getBound(target, 'upper')
                while(propValue < lower | propValue > upper) {
                    if(propValue < lower) propValue <- 2*lower - propValue
                    if(propValue > upper) propValue <- 2*upper - propValue
                }
            }
            model[[target]] <<- propValue
            logMHR <- calculateDiff(model, calcNodes) + propLogScale
            jump <- decide(logMHR)
            if(jump) nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)
            else     nimCopy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)
            if(adaptive & timesRan > niterNoAdaptation)     adaptiveProcedure(jump)
        }
    },
    methods = list(
        adaptiveProcedure = function(jump = logical()) {
            if(jump)     timesAccepted <<- timesAccepted + 1
            if(timesRan %% adaptInterval == 0) {
                acceptanceRate <- timesAccepted / adaptInterval
                if(timesRan > niterNoAdaptiveDecay)   timesAdapted <<- timesAdapted + 1
                gamma1 <<- 1/((timesAdapted + 3)^0.8)
                gamma2 <- 10 * gamma1
                adaptFactor <- exp(gamma2 * (acceptanceRate - optimalAR))
                scale <<- scale * adaptFactor
                timesAccepted <<- 0
            }
        },
        reset = function() {
            scale <<- scaleOriginal
            timesRan      <<- 0
            timesAccepted <<- 0
            timesAdapted  <<- 0
            gamma1 <<- 0
        }
    )
)

code <- nimbleCode({
    a ~ dexp(5)
    b ~ dnorm(a, 1)
})
constants <- list()
data <- list(b = 4)
inits <- list(a = 5)

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code, constants, data, inits)

conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, nodes = NULL)
conf$printSamplers()
conf$addSampler(target = 'a', type = 'RW2', control = list(niterNoAdaptation = 1000))
conf$printSamplers()
Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)

Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

set.seed(0)
samples <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, 10000)

But yes, if we find algorithms that do it automatically it is much better, I agree. I plan to test Jags and Stan on this. I have also tried other algorithms but no clear good result so far.

At least what I can say is that this strategy seems a litlle more promising on the case at hand than Block sampling!

Hi Frédéric

I already have nimble code for the adaptive parallel tempering algorithm of Miasojedow (adapted from NImble's block sampler as it was this time last year).

It was a good challenge getting that sampler working, it took me about 10 days to get it working for a toy problem in population dynamics. I also had to define a virtual nimble function called sampler_APT that replaced the standard sampler_BASE. The sampler worked very nicely for the problem we were tackling, although the adaptive part proved to be not as fool proof as some of Vihola's other adaptive schemes (so I also added some monitors to track what that was doing).

Best
David

Thanks for the question, Frédéric.  It's great to hear how you did it, David.

It sounds like you took a reasonable path.  Some other ideas could include:

- Making a transformation of the model when it is defined so that all log probabilities are adjusted by the temperature.  I think this would involve making the temperature a part of the model itself.

- Making modified versions of sampler nimbleFunctions that could still inherit from sampler_BASE but could be told what the temperature node is via a control parameter.

- Making different sampler objects to be used at different temperatures so that any adaptive parameters adapt to the posterior at that particular temperature (an alternative would be to modify proposal scales based on the temperature).

Those are not all mutually exclusive.  Please keep us up to date on how it goes and whether any of these ideas are of interest.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm learning Nimble and Bayesian state space models with the aim of producing a Poisson state space model with covariates. To start, I've been working on simple regression models in Nimble. I was able to get a basic regression model to work with a single covariate (https://github.com/wccarleton/nimbletesting), but now that I'm trying to extend it to multiple regression, I'm running into trouble. The biggest issue is that I'm getting a C segfault error. I've pasted in my code below (note that I started passing in the precision matrix for the slopes via "Data" as I was troubleshooting another issue, but I think the matrix could be defined in the call to nimbleModel()). Anyone have any ideas what I've done wrong? Does anyone have a working example of multiple regression I could look at?

First the call that throws an error:

lmModel <- nimbleModel(code=lmCode,data=lmData,inits=lmInits,constants=lmConsts)

which returns:

defining model...
Error: segfault from C stack overflow

Now the rest of the code:

#invent some data
x1 <- seq(1,10)*0.005
x2 <- seq(1,10)*0.005
x <- cbind(x1,x2)
y <- 1 + x1*2 + x2*2.5 + rnorm(10,0,sd=0.005)
K <- 2

#create the nimble model
lmCode <- nimbleCode({
   A <- chol(A)
   mMean <- c(0,0)
   intercept ~ dnorm(0, sd=1000)
   slope[1:K] ~ dmnorm(mean=mMean, prec=A)
   sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)
   for (j in 1:N){
      predicted.y[j] <- intercept + t(slope[1:K]) %*% x[j,1:K]
      y[j] ~ dnorm(predicted.y[j], sd=sigma)
   }
})

#create precision matrix
A <- solve(diag(rep(1000,K)))

#data to be passed to nimbleModel()
lmData <- list(y=y,
               x=x,
               A=A)

#constants to be passed to nimbleModel()
lmConsts <- list(N=length(y),
                 K=ncol(x))

#initial paramter settings to be passed to nimbleModel()
lmInits <- list(intercept=1,slope=matrix(c(1,1)),sigma=1)

#create nimble model
lmModel <- nimbleModel(code=lmCode,data=lmData,inits=lmInits,constants=lmConsts)

#compile nimble model to C++ code—much faster runtime
C_lmModel <- compileNimble(lmModel)

#configure the MCMC
lmModel_conf <- configureMCMC(lmModel,print=T)

#select the variables that we want to monitor in the MCMC chain
lmModel_conf$addMonitors(c("intercept","slope","sigma"))

#build the MCMC model
lmModelMCMC <- buildMCMC(lmModel_conf)

#compile MCMC to C++—much faster
C_lmModelMCMC <- compileNimble(lmModelMCMC,project=lmModel)

#number of MCMC iterations
niter=10000

#set seed for replicability
set.seed(1)

#call the C++ compiled MCMC model
C_lmModelMCMC$run(niter)

#save the MCMC chain (monitored variables) as a matrix
samples <- as.matrix(C_lmModelMCMC$mvSamples)

Thanks for the message.

Please try the following version of your model code:

lmCode <- nimbleCode({
    cholA[1:K, 1:K] <- chol(A[1:K, 1:K])

   }
})

There were a few issues.

The BUGS language is declarative, so one can't have something like A <- chol(A).

NIMBLE currently requires very explicit indexing for any non-scalar variable.  An alternative is to provide empty square brackets and use the dimensions argument to nimbleModel if necessary.

NIMBLE is strongly typed, including for dimensions.  The matrix multiplication returns a matrix.  inprod() returns a scalar.

An alternative to the last 4 lines would be:

 predicted.y[1:N] <- intercept + x[1:N, 1:K] %*% slope[1:K]

 for (j in 1:N){

   y[j] ~ dnorm(predicted.y[j], sd=sigma)
 }

-Perry

Hi Chris,

Please try the following code (see comments for explanations):

poisTSCode <- nimbleCode({
    A[1:K,1:K] <- inverse(diag(x = rep(1000,K))) ## nimble version of diag does not accept (or need) more arguments here

   cholA[1:K,1:K] <- chol(A[1:K,1:K])
   multimu[1:K] <- rep(0,K)

   B0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)  ## Note that BUGS parameterization defaults to precision, so you must indicate if you mean std. deviation.

   B[1:K] ~ dmnorm(mean=multimu[1:K], prec=cholA[1:K,1:K])
   mu0 ~ dgamma(a,b)

##   mu[1:T] <- array(0,dim=T)                                  ## It is not valid to declare elements of mu multiple times, so this is not necessary or allowed given that the meaningful declarations are below.
##   mu[1] <- mu0 * exp(B0 + X[1,1:K] %*% B[1:K]) ## The type of the expression on the right-hand size is a matrix, so it cannot be assigned to a scalar.
   mu[1] <- mu0 * exp(B0 + inprod(X[1,1:K], B[1:K]))  ## This works because inprod returns a scalar.

   for (j in 2:T){

      eta[j] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)  ## See comment above.
      ##mu[j] <- mu[j-1] * exp(B0 + X[j,1:K] %*% B[1:K]) * exp(eta[j]) ## See explanation above
      mu[j] <- mu[j-1] * exp(B0 + inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K])) * exp(eta[j])

   }
   for (j in 1:T){
      Y[j] ~ dpois(mu[j])
   }
})

-Perry

Fantastic.  Thanks for digging into that, Chris.  I was just going to sit-down and see if that was the situation.

We aim to release a new version in the next month or so that should include that bug fix.  In the meantime, installing from our devel branch on github is the way to go.

For any other readers wanting to do so, here is how you can, without needing to clone the github repository:

library(devtools)
install_github("nimble-dev/nimble", ref = "devel", subdir = "packages/nimble")

-Perry
